title: AlphaGo's Move 37
hook: The Go move that experts called a mistake, until it won the game.
peek: In 2016, in the second game of its match against Lee Sedol, the program AlphaGo played a move that human experts would almost never consider. Commentators were baffled. It turned out to be the key to the game.
lede: In March 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo played Lee Sedol, one of the strongest Go players in the world, in a five-game match in Seoul. On the 37th move of the second game, it placed a stone on the fifth line from the edge, a spot that convention treats as too loose. Commentators assumed it was an error. By the end, it looked like insight.

bullets.text: AlphaGo's own estimate was that a human player would choose that move about one time in ten thousand. It played it anyway, because its search rated the move's long-term value highly.
Lee took around a quarter of an hour to reply. He went on to lose the game, and AlphaGo won the match four games to one.
In game four, Lee answered with a rare wedge on move 78 that AlphaGo had not expected, and won. Fans gave it a divine nickname, much as cubers speak of God's number.
Go has about 10 to the 170 legal positions, far more than chess. That scale is why experts had expected a win like this to be at least a decade away.
A 2017 film follows the match from both sides, including the DeepMind team and Lee, and shows the reaction in the room when move 37 appeared.
Lee retired from professional Go in 2019. He said the rise of programs that could not be beaten had changed what the game meant to him.
